title: When “Human Error” Is Really a Design Problem
summary: Don Norman's chapter on human error, read for software teams: slips vs mistakes, prod-vs-staging mode errors, forcing functions, undo and root causes without blame.
author: Nguyen Le Phong

book.title: The Design of Everyday Things
book.originalTitle: The Design of Everyday Things; originally published as The Psychology of Everyday Things
book.note: This article is a personal reflection from the revised and expanded edition, focused on ideas that help software and product teams design clearer everyday interactions. It is not a chapter-by-chapter summary.

html:
Say your team has two admin panels, production and staging. Same table, same filters, same blue "Run cleanup" button. The only difference is a small grey label in the top corner. It's 5:40 on a Friday, support has pinged you three times in the last hour, and you run the cleanup in the tab you think is staging. It isn't.

The incident doc gets a first draft by Monday: "Root cause: operator error." That sentence is true, and it's also the least useful thing the team could write. It points at one tired person and leaves the two identical screens exactly where they were, ready for the next person.

Chapter 5 of Don Norman's The Design of Everyday Things has a title that pretty much settles the argument: "Human Error? No, Bad Design." This post reads that chapter (plus a few pages from chapters 4 and 6) with software teams in mind: admin tools, deploy pipelines, payment flows and the incident reviews that follow when they go wrong.

About the book

Don Norman, The Design of Everyday Things, revised and expanded edition (Basic Books, 2013). This post leans on chapter 5 ("Human Error? No, Bad Design"), the forcing-functions part of chapter 4 and the design-thinking chapter 6. It's a set of notes for product and engineering work, so it skips a lot of the book. The companion post on signifiers, mapping and feedback is Screens That Explain Themselves.

Ask why the wrong click made sense

Norman tells this story in his essay "Human Error? No, Bad Design". After a 2013 ferry crash in New York's East River, the first reaction was to blame the captain. The NTSB investigation pointed further back, to confusing control modes on the ferry and weak safety management procedures. Norman's line is that the person at the end of a chain of failures tends to take the blame for problems that started much earlier. His closing advice is to stop blaming people and design for them.

The safety researcher James Reason made the same split in a 2000 paper for the BMJ (Human error: models and management). The "person approach" sees forgetfulness and carelessness, and answers with blame, retraining and more rules. The "system approach" looks at the conditions people work in and builds defenses around them. His summary is worth a sticky note: "We cannot change the human condition, but we can change the conditions under which humans work."

Software teams have a working version of this already. Google's SRE book describes blameless postmortems as starting from the assumption that everyone involved had good intentions and did the right thing with the information they had (Postmortem Culture). The useful question then becomes why the information was incomplete. For the Friday cleanup that gives you a fix list that doesn't depend on anyone's attention at 5:40 p.m.:

  • Put production on its own URL and give it a loud, different look: a red header, the environment name in the page title and on the button itself ("Run cleanup on PRODUCTION").
  • Default risky tools to staging, and make production something you switch into on purpose.
  • Before a destructive action, show the exact records it will touch and how many.
  • Keep the audit log and a restore path, so a bad run is a bad hour and nothing worse.

None of this lets people off the hook. It moves the fix to a level where it protects everyone who opens that panel next month.

Slips and mistakes need different fixes

Norman splits errors into two kinds. A slip is when you meant to do one thing and did another: the goal was right, the action went wrong. A mistake is when the goal or the plan itself was wrong, so even a perfectly executed action takes you somewhere bad. He breaks slips down further into action-based slips and memory lapses, and mistakes into rule-based, knowledge-based and memory-lapse mistakes.

The split matters because the fixes point in different directions. Slips call for better constraints, spacing, defaults and undo. Mistakes call for a clearer model of the system: definitions, examples, and decision support at the moment of choice.

The Friday cleanup is a textbook case of one slip type Norman spends pages on: the mode error. The same controls do different things depending on a state you have to remember. He notes that modes get dangerous exactly when you set one and then get interrupted, or stay in it for a long time. Two browser tabs that differ only by a corner label are a mode error waiting to happen.

Error typeWhat it looks like at workDesign fix that helps
SlipSomeone hits "Archive" while reaching for "Open", because the two buttons sit side by side and look alike.Move the destructive action away, make it look different, add undo.
Slip (mode error)An engineer deploys the right branch to the wrong environment from a dropdown that remembered the last choice.Distinct look per environment, no sticky default for production, show the target and version before confirming.
MistakeA manager reads "active users" as paying customers because the dashboard never defines the term.Put the definition next to the chart and link to how the number is computed.
MistakeSupport runs the normal refund flow on a chargeback, where a different rule applies.Detect the special case, explain why the rule differs, route to the right flow.

Here's the part teams tend to miss: a confirmation dialog checks the action, not the object. If you hit close by accident, the unexpected dialog wakes you up. If you meant to close and simply picked the wrong window, you expected the dialog, so you click through it without reading. Norman uses exactly that example from his own desk: the wrong window closed, nothing saved, possibly a lot of work gone.

Constraints that stop the wrong path

In chapter 4, Norman describes forcing functions: constraints so strong that you can't move on until the right thing has happened. He names three kinds, and each has a direct software cousin.

  • Interlocks force steps into the right order. His example is the microwave that cuts power the moment you open the door. In a pipeline: the production deploy stays locked until the migration has an approved review.
  • Lock-ins keep an operation going so you can't bail out too early, like the app that asks about unsaved work before it quits. In a tool: closing the bulk-send screen halfway through asks whether to finish, pause or cancel the rest, so half a campaign never just vanishes.
  • Lockouts keep you out of a dangerous place. Norman's example is the barrier that stops people running past the ground floor into the basement during a fire. In access control: the person who created a payout batch can't approve it.

Lighter constraints work too. A CSV import can go upload, validate, map columns, preview errors, then commit, so nobody finds out about a broken column after half the rows are already in the database.

Norman also argues for sensibility checks, where the system notices that a value is wildly out of line with what's normal. His example is a money transfer typed into the wrong currency field. For a support tool, that's the refund that's ten times bigger than any refund this agent has ever issued. The system doesn't have to block it. It just has to ask, with the number in plain view.

A design test

When the same error keeps showing up, don't stop at adding a warning. Ask whether you can make the wrong action impossible, harder to reach, more visible, reversible or less damaging. Any one of those beats another yellow banner.

Undo beats "Are you sure?"

Norman calls undo perhaps the most powerful tool for limiting the damage of errors, and says he's still surprised how many systems leave it out where it's clearly possible. His explanation of why "Are you sure?" fails is simple. Right after you ask for an action, you're sure you want it, and you're focused on the action rather than the thing it acts on. So the dialog reads as an irritant and you confirm out of habit.

His two fixes are practical. Make the object of the action prominent: show the actual file, the actual customer or the actual 3,214 records, with the implications spelled out. And make the operation reversible wherever you can.

In business tools that translates to concrete features. A pricing change can be rolled back. A content editor can restore last week's version. A support email sits in a send queue for a minute and can be cancelled. Archive with restore comes before a hard delete. When undo really isn't possible, say so on the screen and slow that one action down with specifics, such as making the person type the name of the environment.

Checklists hold the steps you'd forget

Interruptions break memory. Norman says checklists cut errors, especially slips and memory lapses, and matter most in complex work full of interruptions. Two of his details are easy to skip and worth stealing. First, a checklist works better when two people run it together, one reading and one doing, than when one person does it and a second checks later, because each starts trusting the other to catch things. Second, a lot of people who say they hate checklists actually hate badly designed ones.

He also likes electronic checklists because they can track skipped items and refuse to mark the list complete until everything is done. That fits software well. If the migration review is missing, the deploy button stays grey. If no one owns the feature flag, the launch task stays open.

Keep the list short and real. Six items people actually check beat thirty that everyone clicks through. If you want more on keeping lists next to the work they guard, see Keep Checklists Close to the Work.

Keep asking why after the first answer

Norman describes the Five Whys, which came from Sakichi Toyoda and the Toyota Production System: when you find a reason, ask why that was the case, and keep going. The number isn't magic. The name is there to stop you from quitting after the first answer. Run it on the Friday cleanup:

  • Why did the cleanup hit production? The engineer was in the production tab.
  • Why did that look like staging? Both panels share a layout and the label is tiny.
  • Why was the production tab open at all? Support work needs both environments open side by side.
  • Why is the destructive button on the support screen? Nobody split read-only tools from write tools.

Now you're learning something. Norman is honest about the method's limits: "why" is ambiguous, people stop when they hit the edge of their own understanding, and it nudges you toward a single cause when most incidents have several. Reason's Swiss cheese model fills that gap. Every layer of defense has holes, and an accident happens when the holes in several layers line up. So a good review lists every layer that let the problem through.

What happenedThe deeper design questionPossible system fix
A payment got captured twiceWhy did retrying feel safe while the first request was still pending?Idempotency key, a visible pending state, the retry button disabled until the first call settles.
A campaign went to the wrong customersWhy was checking recipients so weak in a high-impact flow?Recipient preview with a count, a test send first, a short undo window before the bulk send.
Production data changed by accidentWhy did production look and behave like staging?Distinct styling, an explicit switch into production, write permissions split from read, a preview of affected rows.

For how to run the review itself without anyone getting thrown under the bus, the culture side is in A Blameless Culture Starts in the First Minute of the Postmortem.

Solve the problem behind the request

Chapter 6 opens with "Solving the Correct Problem". Norman's point is that the problem you're handed is often a symptom. Human-centered design, in his telling, is hands-on work: watch what people really do, figure out the real problem, prototype cheaply, test, repeat.

Product teams get symptom requests all the time. "Add a confirmation dialog" might really mean two dangerous actions look identical. "Write a training page" might mean the product uses three words for the same thing. "Add more dashboard filters" might mean nobody agreed on what decision the dashboard supports.

A rough prototype settles this faster than a long thread. Put the risky flow in front of a few people who do the job, give them a realistic task and watch where they slow down. Often the missing piece is small: a state label, a preview, a safer default or a way back.

Complex is fine, confusing isn't

One section title in chapter 6 is a whole design philosophy: "Complexity Is Good; It Is Confusion That Is Bad." Norman's example is the kitchen. Someone else's kitchen feels chaotic, yours feels obvious, and the difference is knowledge, not the number of drawers. His fix for taming complexity is a good conceptual model, so people understand why things are where they are.

That matters for tools like payroll setup, Kubernetes dashboards and tax flows, which are complex because the work is. Ripping out every advanced control makes a cleaner screenshot and a weaker tool. Help people find their way instead: group related controls, reveal advanced options when they're needed, show the current state, keep defaults safe.

Norman also has a name for the opposite failure, in chapter 7: "featuritis", whose main symptom is creeping featurism. Each new option looks harmless alone. Together they blur the model until nobody can predict what the product will do. Before adding a feature, check whether it strengthens the core task or just adds one more thing to learn.

Try this week

  • Open your production admin and staging side by side. If you can't tell them apart in two seconds, file a ticket.
  • Find one "Are you sure?" dialog and replace it with undo, or with a preview of exactly what will change.
  • In your next incident review, ask "why did this make sense at the time?" before anyone writes "human error".
  • Label each error in your last two incidents as a slip or a mistake, then check the fix matches the type.
  • Cut your release checklist to the items people actually verify, and wire one of them into the pipeline.

The best part of this chapter is how ordinary the fixes are. A safer default, a red header on production, an undo window, a shorter checklist. None of them look impressive on a roadmap, and each one means the next tired person on a Friday afternoon doesn't have to be perfect.

faqs.q: What does Don Norman mean by “Human Error? No, Bad Design”?
faqs.a: It's the title of chapter 5 in the 2013 edition of The Design of Everyday Things. Norman argues that the person at the end of a chain of failures usually takes the blame for problems that began earlier, in confusing designs and weak procedures. The useful fix is to change the design so the same error gets less likely or less costly.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a slip and a mistake?
faqs.a: A slip is when the goal is right but the action goes wrong, like clicking Archive while reaching for Open. A mistake is when the goal or plan is wrong from the start, like applying the normal refund rule to a chargeback. Slips need constraints, spacing and undo. Mistakes need a clearer model of the system and better decision support.

faqs.q: What is a mode error in software?
faqs.a: A mode error happens when the same controls do different things depending on a state you have to remember. Production and staging admin panels that look identical are a classic case. Norman notes modes get dangerous when people are interrupted or stay in one mode for a long time, so make each mode look clearly different.

faqs.q: What are forcing functions in UX?
faqs.a: Forcing functions are constraints that stop you from moving on until the right step is done. Norman describes three kinds in chapter 4: interlocks (steps in the right order), lock-ins (don't quit an operation too early) and lockouts (keep people out of a dangerous state). A production deploy locked until the migration is reviewed is an interlock.

faqs.q: Why is undo often better than a confirmation dialog?
faqs.a: Right after asking for an action, people are sure they want it and focus on the action, so they confirm out of habit. Norman suggests making the affected object prominent and making the action reversible. Keep confirmations for actions that truly can't be undone, and make them specific about what will change.
